newsitem.title: GERMANY: GRUNDIG, PHILIPS HOPE FOR PEACEFUL DIVORCE.
newsitem.headline: GRUNDIG, PHILIPS HOPE FOR PEACEFUL DIVORCE.

text.p: Troubled German electonics maker Grundig [GRNG.CN] and its former parent Philips Electronics said on Thursday they hoped to resolve amicably a dispute over more than 800 million marks ($488.2 million) in divorce payments.

Grundig said it was checking for legal grounds to recoup some losses incurred before Philips gave up control of the company on January 1. It said the companies continue to talk regularly but had not entered formal negotiations.
"We are in standing contact with Philips. There is no confrontation," Grundig spokesman Thomas Meckeleit told Reuters. "There can be no negotiations until we check our legal position."

Grundig raised the possibility of legal recourse on Monday when Philips-appointed chief executive Pieter van der Wal resigned under employee protests against his plan to lay off a third of Grundig's 8,500 workers.
Van der Wal had already cut 4,000 jobs in the last year and planned to move television production out of Germany.

The Dutch electronics group, which owns 32 percent of Grundig and ran the company under a contract with the Max Grundig Foundation, shared "the hope Grundig and Philips reach a settlement on friendly terms," a spokesman in Eindhoven said.

Despite the potential legal scuffle, Grundig planned to move its new strategy forward on Friday by introducing a consulting firm charged with finding a business partner to replace Philips, Meckeleit said.
Grundig's lawyers should have a better idea on whether Philips was obliged to pay part of the 800 million marks back a few days later, Meckeleit said.
"A clarification on the legal situation between Grundig and Philips should come soon," he said. "The situation between Philips and the Max Grundig Foundation will take longer."

The dispute involves some 500 million marks Grundig lost in 1994 and 1995, when Philips was covering the German company's losses as part of its agreement with the Grundig foundation, which owns 68 percent of Grundig.

Grundig said it believed Philips still has to pay the sum. Philips maintained it has taken the roll of a "passive shareholder" and that its actions are covered by escape clauses in its management agreement.
Grundig also hoped to recover 250 million marks it paid to Philips earlier this month to cancel Philips' options to raise its stake to 50.5 percent.
Also in dispute was 80 million marks Grundig contended Philips improperly transferred from Grundig subsidiaries to minimize the loss Philips would have to cover for 1996.

Grundig lost 350 million marks on about 3.3 billion marks in sales last year, company sources said, but it was not immediately clear whether Grundig would also seek compensation from Philips for these losses as well.

While Grundig was trying to clarify the legal basis of its claims, Philips, which lost 1.5 billion marks on Grunding between 1984 and 1996, maintained that the only open questions concern its ties to the foundation.

"From January 1 we have been a passive minority shareholder in Grundig," a spokesman said. "We've given up control and have held negotiations with the Max Grundig foundation about winding up the contractual relationship which covers among other things the annual dividend" to the foundation.
"We also want to discuss the put option the foundation has to sell to Philips their 68 percent stake for 540 million German marks," he said.
